docs.title: Expense Bot
docs.text:
A personal Telegram bot for tracking expenses. You text it what you spent and it logs it; you ask about your spending and it answers.

This site documents how it was built and what I learned building it.

Code: github.com/DanielAsenso-G/expense-bot

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Send a message like "spent 40 on lunch" and the bot pulls out the amount and category, saves it, and replies with a short confirmation. Ask something like "how much have I spent this week?" and it reads your logged expenses and answers.

The bot distinguishes logging from asking: a logged expense gets a short acknowledgement, a question gets a full answer.

Logging expenses, then asking for a breakdown.

docs.title: Around this site
docs.text:
• How it works — the architecture and request flow.
  • How it was built — the build, phase by phase.
  • What I learned — the concepts and lessons, by theme.

docs.title: How it was built
docs.text: The project was built in deliberate phases, each ending in something that runs and can be checked — foundations (the "pipe") before features (the "water").

docs.title: Phase 0 — Plan & scope
docs.text: Started from an enterprise WhatsApp integration design and deliberately cut it down to a minimal, personal spec — deciding each trade-off (one capability, SQLite over Postgres, the cheapest LLM, a single service) rather than inheriting them.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Bot + first message by hand
docs.text: Created the bot and sent a message to myself by hand with curl — proving the external piece worked before writing any server code. (Originally targeted WhatsApp, but pivoted to Telegram after Meta's business-verification wall blocked a personal account. The architecture was channel-agnostic, so the switch was cheap.)

docs.title: Phase 2 — Repo + running server
docs.text: Scaffolded the project (Poetry, git, a gitignored .env), wrote a minimal FastAPI server with a health route, ran it locally, and pushed it to GitHub.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Webhook: receive + verify
docs.text: Exposed the local server with an ngrok tunnel, registered a webhook with Telegram, received real messages, and verified each request with a secret token — rejecting anything that isn't really from Telegram with a 403.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Outbound reply
docs.text:
Closed the loop: the bot replies by calling Telegram's sendMessage API with httpx. The first version just echoed messages back, to prove the round trip worked.

The first working loop — the bot echoing messages back.

docs.title: Phase 5 — The brain
docs.text:
Added the real logic:

  • a SQLite table for expenses,
  • Gemini to parse free text into {amount, category, note},
  • storage (add_expense) and reads (get_expenses),
  • a router that classifies each message as a log or an ask,
  • and an answer path that reads the data and responds.

This is the functional MVP: the bot logs expenses and answers questions about them, end to end.

The finished flow: logging expenses and answering a question from the stored data.

docs.title: Phase 6 — Polish
docs.text: README, this documentation site, the system-design diagram, screenshots, and deployment.

docs.title: Planned next
docs.text: Give the LLM today's date / compute per-day totals in SQL (let the database do the math), handle non-text messages, add edit/delete, Excel export, and a hosted deployment.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Text the bot and it routes your message: one that records spending is logged, a question about spending is answered.

flowchart TD
    User(["You"]) -->|message| TCI["Telegram app"]
    TCI --> TG["Telegram servers"]
    TG -->|"webhook POST"| WH

    subgraph App["Your FastAPI server (expense-bot)"]
        WH["Webhook: verify secret"] --> C{"log or ask?"}
        C -->|log| P["parse_expense"]
        P --> A["add_expense"]
        A --> DB[("SQLite")]
        C -->|ask| R["get_expenses"]
        DB --> R
        R --> Ans["answer_question"]
        A --> Rep["send reply"]
        Ans --> Rep
    end

    P -.->|"parse via LLM"| G["Gemini API"]
    Ans -.->|"answer via LLM"| G
    Rep -->|"sendMessage"| TG
    TG -->|reply| TCI
    TCI --> User

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
1. You send a message in Telegram.
  2. Telegram POSTs it to the bot's webhook (a FastAPI endpoint), which verifies a secret token to confirm the request really came from Telegram.
  3. The bot classifies the message as a log or an ask (using Gemini).
  4. Log: Gemini parses the message into {amount, category, note}, it's stored in SQLite, and the bot replies with a short confirmation.
  5. Ask: the bot reads the stored expenses from SQLite, and Gemini answers the question using that data.
  6. The reply goes back to Telegram via the Bot API.

docs.title: Stack
docs.text:
• Python + FastAPI — the webhook server (the receiving side).
  • SQLite — stores the expenses.
  • Google Gemini — parses messages, classifies intent, and answers questions.
  • ngrok — exposes the local server to the internet during development.

Inbound webhook requests are verified with a Telegram secret token, so only Telegram can reach the bot.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
I came into this comfortable with Python but having never connected anything to the outside world — I'd never built an API integration, set up a webhook, or used a database for anything real. I learned all of it by building this bot in small steps, and these pages are a reflection on what actually stuck, roughly in the order it started to make sense to me.

A couple of ideas ran through the whole project. The biggest was to build in a deliberate order: get the plumbing working and verifiable before adding anything clever — a repo, then a server that runs, then one that can receive, then one that replies, and only then the actual logic. Every step ended in something I could check, so I was never debugging five new things at once.

The other is to avoid tying yourself to things you don't control. Partway in, Meta's WhatsApp setup locked me out behind business verification I couldn't complete, and instead of fighting it I moved the whole bot to Telegram in an afternoon — because I'd kept the messaging channel separate from the logic, so swapping it was cheap. That separation turned out to be the most useful decision I made.

The rest is grouped by topic:

  • APIs & HTTP — how programs talk to each other
  • Webhooks & networking — how Telegram reaches my laptop
  • Databases & SQL — how the bot remembers
  • LLMs — the part that understands and answers
  • Secrets, Git & tooling — the workflow around it all

docs.title: APIs & HTTP
docs.text:
Before this, "API" was a word I used without really having a picture for it. The one that finally worked was a menu. When my code talks to Telegram, I don't get to reach into their servers and poke around — I order from a fixed list of things they let me ask for (send a message, fetch updates, set a webhook), in exactly the format they specify. That menu is the API: a contract between two programs, where one side exposes a set of requests and keeps everything behind them hidden. Once I noticed every call follows the same shape — https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/<method> — the whole thing felt a lot less like magic.

What took longer to sink in was that "client" and "server" aren't fixed labels; they're roles that swap depending on who starts the conversation. When my bot sends a message, it's the client calling Telegram's server. When Telegram pushes a message to my bot, Telegram is the client and my code is the server. Same two parties, opposite roles, depending on which way the request is flowing.

GET and POST confused me for a while, because I assumed the type was somehow worked out from what the request did. It isn't. It's just a word the sender writes at the start of the request — GET if you're reading something, POST if you're sending data along in the body. And that's a convention, not a rule the machine enforces: Telegram will happily let you "set" a webhook with a GET even though it clearly changes something. That bugged me until I accepted that the label is just the sender's declaration, nothing more.

The last piece was realising a response is really two things: a status code and a body. The code is a quick summary of how it went — 200 fine, 403 not allowed, 404 nothing at this address, 422 you sent something malformed, 500 it broke — and the body is the actual content that comes back. A 404 stopped feeling like "broken" once I understood it just means the server is alive and simply has nothing at the address I asked for.

docs.title: Databases & SQL
docs.text:
The bot was useless until it could remember things. Before that, anything it "knew" lived in memory and vanished the moment the program restarted — RAM is temporary. To remember expenses across days, I had to write them to disk, and a database is just an organised way to do that.

The model that made databases click was a spreadsheet. A database holds tables; a table has columns (the fields — amount, category, a note, a date) and rows (one per expense). The shape of those columns is the schema, and you talk to the whole thing in SQL, a language that reads almost like English (SELECT, INSERT, and so on).

I used SQLite, which is a full database that lives in a single file with no separate server to run — the same thing that quietly runs inside phones and browsers. The alternative, something like Postgres, runs as its own service that many apps connect to over a network; that's what you reach for once you have lots of users (and you'd add a column to tag whose data is whose). For one person and one file, SQLite is perfect.

The most useful habit I picked up was designing the table backwards from the questions I'd ask it. I knew I'd want "how much, on what, and when", so the columns almost wrote themselves. I also learned to be deliberate about constraints — amount and category are required, but the note is optional, so I left it nullable.

Two things about writing to it stuck with me. First, changes aren't saved until you commit() — until then they're staged, a bit like edits you haven't hit save on. Second, you never paste values straight into a SQL string. If you did, a mischievous note like '); DROP TABLE expenses;-- could be read as a command and wipe the table — that's SQL injection. Instead you leave ? placeholders and hand the values over separately, so the database always treats them as data, never code (it also quietly handles awkward characters like apostrophes, which would otherwise break the query).

Reading data back introduced the cursor — running a SELECT hands you a pointer into the results that you pull rows out of with fetchall(). The one trap I hit: you have to fetch the rows before you close the connection, because the cursor reads from the connection you just shut.

I also brushed up against migrations — the idea that once a table holds real data, you can't just rewrite its definition; you change it carefully with ALTER TABLE so you don't lose what's there. I didn't need one this time, but it's good to know the live schema isn't something you edit casually.

docs.title: LLMs
docs.text:
The LLM is the part that makes the bot feel smart — it turns "spent 36 at akornor on rice and stew" into neat fields, and it answers questions in plain English. Using it was simpler than I expected: you create a client once, then hand it a model name and a prompt. The surprising part was that each call is completely stateless — the model remembers nothing between calls. What feels like memory in a chatbot is an illusion created by resending the whole conversation every time (even talking to Claude works that way).

The thing that tripped me up most wasn't the model, it was JSON. I kept thinking JSON and a Python dictionary were the same thing — they look identical. They're not: JSON is text, a dict is a live object in memory. Since you can only send text over a network, Gemini hands back JSON text, and I parse it into a dict with json.loads. To stop the model wrapping its reply in stray formatting, I ask for JSON explicitly, which guarantees something I can actually parse.

A principle I'll keep: match the tool to the job. The LLM is great at language — reading messy human text, writing a friendly summary — but I don't trust it to do arithmetic. Numbers should come from the database, which actually computes them; the model's job is to phrase the answer, not add things up.

Routing is where log and ask come together. Each message first goes to the model with one question — is this logging an expense or asking about spending? — and the answer decides the path. I learned to make that check forgiving: if the reply is anything other than a clean "ask", I treat it as a log, so an odd response never leaves the user with silence. On the ask side, I feed the stored expenses and the question to the model with no JSON constraint this time, because now I want natural language back, not structured data.

docs.title: Secrets, Git & tooling
docs.text: This is the scaffolding around the actual bot — the habits and tools that make it a real project rather than a throwaway script.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: The one rule I drilled into myself: secrets never go in the code or the repo. The bot token and API keys live in a .env file that git ignores, and the code reads them from the environment at runtime. I commit a .env.example with the names but no values, so anyone cloning the repo knows what to supply. I also learned to check git status before committing — and that if a secret ever leaks, you rotate it immediately rather than hope nobody noticed (I did exactly that after pasting my bot token by accident). For generating one, openssl rand -hex 32 gives you something genuinely unguessable.

docs.title: Git, and juggling two accounts
docs.text: What finally clarified git for me was separating two "identities" I'd been treating as one. There's who wrote a commit (set with git config user.name/email), and there's which account is allowed to push (handled by SSH keys). I keep separate work and personal GitHub accounts, so I use an SSH host alias to make sure pushes from this project land on the personal one, plus a GitHub noreply email to keep my real address out of public history. And it all stays local until you push — init, add, commit happen on my machine; GitHub only hears about it when I push.

docs.title: Python and the toolchain
docs.text: Poetry manages the project's dependencies and its virtual environment — an isolated set of packages just for this project, so it never clashes with anything else, with exact versions pinned so the setup is reproducible. A few smaller things I now actually understand rather than copy: poetry run executes a command inside that environment; __init__.py marks a folder as an importable package; and an import like expense_bot.db means the db.py module inside the expense_bot package — not to be confused with expenses.db, which is the data file.

docs.title: FastAPI
docs.text: FastAPI is the framework that receives requests; uvicorn is the server that runs it and listens on a port — the recipe and the cook. A route like @app.get("/health") just registers a function to handle requests to that path. The neat part is that FastAPI fills in your function's arguments from the right place based on their type — a dict comes from the request body, a header from Header(...) — so you declare what you want and it hands it over. It also generates interactive API docs at /docs for free.

docs.title: The terminal
docs.text: Most of my friction was the shell, not the code. I learned to quote URLs so characters like ? and & aren't misread, that < > and [] mean special things to the shell, and that a long one-liner pastes more reliably than a multi-line command. The curl flags make sense now too: -X sets the method, -H adds a header, -d sends a body. Small stuff, but it's the difference between fighting the terminal and using it.

docs.title: Webhooks & networking
docs.text:
There are two ways to get messages from Telegram, and the difference is who does the work. I could poll — keep asking "anything new?" over and over — or I could set up a webhook and have Telegram push each message to me the instant it arrives. The webhook is the better deal: instead of me pestering them, they call me.

But "they call me" raises a question I hadn't thought about — call me where? A webhook is an endpoint I host: a URL Telegram sends each new message to. Which means the roles flip. Normally my code is the client calling Telegram, but for the webhook, Telegram is the client and my little server is the one being called. And Telegram doesn't learn anything about my setup — it just sends a fixed, documented shape to whatever URL I register, and it's on me to read it.

One thing I only really understood by watching it happen: a webhook wants a quick "200 OK" back, and if it doesn't get one it assumes delivery failed and retries later. At one point my connection was slow, messages piled up, and the moment it recovered a burst of them flushed through all at once. That was the retry behaviour, live.

Because that URL is public, anything could POST to it pretending to be Telegram. So I register a secret token, Telegram echoes it back in a header on every request, and my code checks it — anything that doesn't match gets rejected with a 403. (The message itself rides in the request body; the secret rides in a header — two different parts of the same request.)

The part that genuinely surprised me was realising my laptop can't just be reached from the internet. It sits behind my router on a private address, and the router blocks anything trying to start a conversation from outside. Outbound works — that's why I can browse and send API calls — but nothing can reach in. So how does a webhook get to a server running on my own machine?

That's what ngrok is for. It opens an outbound connection from my laptop to its own public server, then relays anything that hits that public URL back down to me — a temporary stand-in for a real address, just for development. When you actually deploy, a host runs your code on a machine that already has its own public address, and the tunnel isn't needed anymore.

A few smaller things settled along the way: localhost and 127.0.0.1 are the same thing, just "this computer"; and one machine has many ports — numbered doors, one per program (my server on 8000, ngrok's inspector on 4040). And when a curl once timed out with "failed to connect", I learned to read that as a network problem rather than a bug — my home wifi was quietly blocking Telegram, and a phone hotspot fixed it.
